s: Part five.
Human review and confidence.
By the end of this part, you'll know when a model's confidence number means something, why averages hide failures, and how three kinds of human review fit together.
Let's start with a picture.
A weather forecaster says "ninety percent chance of rain."
That's something checkable.
Write down every day they said ninety.
Count how many were wet.
If it comes out near nine in ten, the number means what it says.
If it comes out at six in ten?
The forecaster said it with the same conviction.
And you've learned the number cannot carry the weight you were about to put on it.
That tally is calibration.
It's something you measure against what happened afterwards.
It is not something the forecaster can hand you along with the forecast.
A model's stated confidence is similar.
With one difference.
The forecaster is scored, and knows it.
A model that writes "confidence zero point nine" has not been scored on anything.
The number is a claim, produced by the same process that produced the answer.
It's often useful.
And often in the right order.
Items marked point nine usually are more reliable than items marked point seven.
But none of that makes point nine mean ninety percent.
In exam terms.
A stated confidence is a token sequence, not a measured probability.
Until it has been measured against outcomes.
A signal is calibrated when its stated level matches the observed frequency of correctness.
How do you establish that?
Take a labelled sample, meaning items where you know the right answer.
Bucket them by stated confidence.
And compute accuracy per bucket.
There are two common findings.
First.
The mapping is monotonic but compressed.
So point seven and point nine five do separate the population.
But point nine five might mean eighty-two percent in practice.
Second.
The mapping differs by input type.
Once you have that table, you set a threshold to a stated target error rate.
And you re-measure whenever the inputs change.
Choosing point nine because it sounds high is, in the notes' phrase, not calibration but decoration.
The second idea is segmentation.
The plain version.
A train line runs ninety-four percent on time.
It can still have one service that is late every single morning.
If that's your train, ninety-four percent describes someone else's life.
In exam terms, report accuracy by document type, and by intake channel.
And show the volume of each segment alongside its accuracy.
An average across types that behave differently hides the one that fails.
The notes' example.
Ninety-eight percent on native digital invoices.
Ninety-six on clean scans.
And sixty-one on scanned handwritten notes, which are six percent of volume.
The average barely moves.
And every reviewer who handles handwritten notes stops trusting the whole system.
Quick recap before the questions.
Confidence means nothing until counted against outcomes.
And accuracy has to be reported per segment, with volumes.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
An invoice pipeline will auto-post any extraction with self-reported confidence of point nine or higher.
The threshold was chosen after a random two-hundred-document evaluation showed ninety-five percent accuracy overall.
The volume is eighty percent native invoices in Portable Document Format, or PDF.
Fifteen percent scanned receipts.
And five percent handwritten delivery notes.
Finance allows at most two percent error on auto-posted items.
What should happen before go-live?
Take a second.
The answer.
Label a sample stratified by document type.
Measure accuracy per confidence bucket within each type.
And set per-type thresholds to the two percent target.
Stratified means you deliberately draw enough from each type, oversampling the small ones.
And here's the give-away number.
A random sample of two hundred contains only about ten handwritten notes.
So the aggregate can hide a failing segment.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: go live, because ninety-five percent overall looks fine.
Why?
That's the averaging mistake, with an untested threshold.
Wrong: raise the global threshold to point nine seven.
Why?
It's still uncalibrated.
It raises review cost everywhere.
And it may still admit a bad handwritten segment.
Wrong: ask the model to justify each score in a sentence, and auto-post only if it cites fields.
Why?
The justification comes from the same process as the score.
It establishes no link to correctness.
The notes add a few more wrong answers in the same family.
Leadership asks for the false-negative rate on unreviewed items, and nobody can produce it.
What's wrong here?
Wrong: report the average stated confidence as a proxy.
Wrong: raise the threshold, to shrink the unreviewed pile.
Wrong: switch on extended thinking, so confidence becomes "better grounded."
Why are all three wrong?
Because only measurement against outcomes establishes the relationship.
One more from the notes.
A pipeline reports ninety-four percent, but adjusters re-key claims by hand.
The first step is to segment the accuracy, with volumes.
Wrong: increase the sample size.
Why?
It just tightens the interval around the wrong statistic.
Wrong, at least as a first step: add a second extraction pass and flag disagreements.
Why?
It's a legitimate technique.
But it doubles cost, and skips the diagnosis of which inputs are systematically hard.
Takeaway.
A confidence number means nothing until you have counted it against outcomes, per input type, against a target you stated.
The next concept is choosing a review design.
There are three.
And the exam wants you to know what each buys.
The plain version.
You can check every piece of work before it goes out.
You can let confident work through automatically, and check the doubtful ones.
Or you can spot-check a random handful from every category, to see how the whole operation is doing.
They sound like alternatives.
They are actually three different jobs.
In exam terms.
Let's take them one at a time.
One.
Review everything.
Choose it for irreversible or regulated decisions, a brand-new pipeline, or no labelled data yet.
It's the most expensive, and it scales with volume.
Its residual risk is reviewer fatigue.
Review turns into rubber-stamping.
So measured accuracy drifts up, while real accuracy does not.
Two.
Stratified sampling.
Choose it when you need an unbiased accuracy estimate per segment.
Especially for low-volume, high-risk types.
The cost is moderate and predictable.
Its residual risk is that individual bad outputs still ship.
Because sampling measures the system, rather than gating items.
Three.
Confidence-thresholded review.
Choose it only once confidence has been calibrated against outcomes.
It's the cheapest per item.
And it concentrates spend on the uncertain tail.
Its residual risk is that confidently wrong items pass unseen.
And calibration drifts silently as inputs change.
The mature design runs all three at once.
Why?
Because their roles do not overlap.
Thresholding gates individual items.
Stratified sampling audits the population.
Including the items thresholding let through.
That's the only way to see that a threshold has gone stale.
Full review is reserved for the segments and action classes where one error costs more than reviewing them all.
And whatever any of the three learns feeds back into the thresholds and routing.
Hold on to this line.
A review workflow with no feedback path is just an expensive delay.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
A brand-new multi-agent system drafts regulatory-change briefings, which compliance officers file with a regulator.
There is no labelled accuracy data.
Leadership wants to auto-approve any briefing on which three independent agent runs agree.
What should happen?
Take a second.
The answer.
Review every briefing at launch, and record the verdicts.
Those verdicts build the labelled set that later justifies calibrated thresholds and sampling.
That's how full review stops being permanent.
And notice, three conditions each independently point to full review.
Regulated output.
A new pipeline.
No labels.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: auto-approve when three runs agree.
Why?
Runs sharing the same criteria share the same blind spots.
Unanimity is not correctness.
Wrong: auto-approve above a synthesis confidence of point eight.
Why?
That number has never been measured against anything.
Wrong: review a five percent random sample, while the rest goes to the regulator.
Why?
That measures the system, but lets individual bad briefings through.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A claims pipeline already has calibrated per-type thresholds.
Only below-threshold items go to review.
Reviewer capacity is fixed at about ten percent of volume.
A new insurer template arrives next quarter.
And the team fears the thresholds will quietly go stale.
What should they do?
Take a second.
The answer.
Audit a stratified random sample of the auto-accepted items, per document type, oversampling the new template.
And feed the labels back into the thresholds.
That fits inside capacity.
In the example, roughly seven percent on the gate, and two percent on the audit.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: route everything to review for a quarter.
Why?
It blows the capacity, and invites rubber-stamping.
Wrong: track the weekly average stated confidence of auto-accepted items.
Why?
It can stay high while accuracy falls.
And confidently wrong items are exactly what a confidence monitor cannot see.
Wrong: raise every threshold by a fixed safety margin.
Why?
It's a global remedy without measurement.
It raises cost everywhere, and still produces no error rate.
So, threshold versus sampling versus full review.
Thresholds decide about each item.
Sampling tells you whether the thresholds are still true.
Full review is for where one mistake is too expensive to risk.
And for the start, when you have nothing to calibrate against.
And the stem words that flip it.
"Regulated," "new," "no labelled data."
Those point to full review.
"Fixed reviewer capacity," and "drift" or "new template."
Those point to a stratified audit of what was auto-accepted.
"Chosen because it felt right," or "cannot state the false-negative rate."
Those point to calibration on a labelled sample.
That's part five.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Thresholds gate items, sampling audits the gate, full review covers what you cannot yet trust, and every verdict feeds back.
The notes close this part with a bridge to the next.
The most useful thing you can hand a reviewer is not a confidence number.
It is the evidence.
Coming up in part six: provenance and uncertainty in multi-source synthesis.
